what: Nexstar Media Group owns local television stations — more of them than anyone else in the United States. Its stations carry the major network programmes in their cities, produce local news, and it also owns The CW network and the news channel NewsNation.
customers: Two very different payers: advertisers buying local airtime, and cable, satellite and streaming distributors who must pay Nexstar to carry its stations.
money: Retransmission fees paid by pay-television distributors for the right to carry Nexstar’s stations.
Local and national advertising, including political advertising in election years.
moat: Broadcast licences are issued by the regulator and strictly limited, so the number of stations in any city is fixed. A distributor that wants the local network affiliate has no alternative source for it, which is why retransmission fees can be raised at each renewal. Owning stations in many markets also makes Nexstar the counterparty the networks and distributors must negotiate with.
risks: Pay-television subscribers keep falling, and retransmission revenue is a fee per subscriber. The rate rises but the subscriber count shrinks, and eventually the second wins.
Revenue swings with the political cycle: $5.4B in 2024 with election advertising, $4.9B in 2025 without it. Comparing consecutive years is misleading.
Debt is about $6.6B against $280.0M of cash, which is more than the equity is worth at the current price.
Local advertising is losing share to digital platforms year after year, a structural decline rather than a cyclical one.
Ownership rules cap how many stations one company may own, which limits consolidation unless the regulator relaxes them.
opportunities: Free cash flow of about $1.3B against a $6.2B market value is an extraordinary yield, and the shares trade at about 4.8 times free cash flow.
Retransmission fees are contracted and renegotiated upward, which makes a large share of revenue predictable for years at a time.
Political advertising is growing with every cycle, and Nexstar’s stations sit in many of the contested states where that money is spent.
The cash is being used to buy back stock aggressively, which shrinks the share count against a declining but highly cash-generative business.
Eight analysts average a $245.38 target, about 23% above the current price.
watch: Net subscriber losses at the pay-television distributors against the rate increase per subscriber. That arithmetic decides when retransmission revenue peaks, and everything about this investment follows from it.
view: Local television is a melting ice cube that produces an enormous amount of water on the way down, and the whole question with Nexstar is how long the melting takes and what you are paying for the water. At 4.8 times free cash flow, the market is pricing a fairly rapid melt. The company generates about $1.3 billion of free cash against a $6.2 billion market value, and is using it to buy back stock, which means the per-share figures improve even as the business shrinks. That is a legitimate way to make money, and it is what the shareholders here are actually betting on.

The structure of the revenue is what makes it work for now. Slightly more than half comes from retransmission fees — cable, satellite and streaming distributors paying Nexstar for the right to carry the local network affiliate. That is contracted, negotiated every few years, and goes up each time, because a distributor that wants the local NBC or CBS station in a city has exactly one place to get it. Broadcast licences are limited by regulation, so no competitor can appear. It is a genuine monopoly, on a shrinking base.

The shrinking base is the bear case and it is arithmetic rather than opinion: the fee is per subscriber, and pay-television subscribers keep leaving. For years the rate increases have outrun the subscriber losses. At some point they stop doing so, and the moment they do, the most predictable half of this company’s revenue turns from growing to declining. Nobody can tell you exactly when; you can watch it quarter by quarter, which is why that is the number to follow rather than earnings.

Two things make the current price more interesting than the usual declining-media story. First, the political advertising cycle is real money and it grows every election, and Nexstar owns stations in a lot of the places where that money gets spent — which is also why comparing 2025 against 2024 makes the business look worse than it is. Second, $6.6 billion of debt against a $6.2 billion market value means this is a leveraged equity: the free cash flow services it comfortably today, and if the melt accelerates the lenders are ahead of the shareholders. That leverage cuts both ways and it is the reason the multiple is so low. I would own this only with a clear view that the buyback outruns the decline, and I would check the subscriber math every quarter.
bull: Retransmission rate increases keep outrunning subscriber losses, political advertising grows each cycle, and the buyback compounds per-share value out of a 4.8 times free cash flow multiple.
bear: Pay-television losses overtake the rate increases, the most predictable half of revenue starts shrinking, and $6.6 billion of debt sits ahead of the equity.
